lead: USB is a host-controlled serial bus that replaced messy parallel ports for keyboards, cameras and printers. A host schedules every transfer through a tiered star of hubs, supplies bus power, and uses four transfer types matched to timing needs. Parallel interfaces move many bits at once with handshake lines. Centronics and IEEE 1284 printer ports use STROBE, BUSY and ACK; GPIO parallel ports drive LCDs and keypads. Embedded products use USB for PC links and charging, and parallel ports for simple local devices.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for serial versus parallel and framing; see Unit 1 for processor and interface choices.

sections.h3: USB is a host-controlled, tiered star

blocks.text: USB is a serial bus built around one host. The host owns the bus and starts every transaction; devices answer only when addressed. The physical layout is a tiered star: the host connects to a root hub, hubs branch to more hubs or devices, and the tree can hold up to 127 devices. No device talks directly to another device; all data passes through the host.

Each device exposes endpoints. An endpoint is a buffer with a direction and a transfer type; endpoint 0 is always present for control. Direction names are from the host's view: IN means device-to-host, OUT means host-to-device.

Four transfer types exist because one bus must carry a mouse (small, urgent), a file (large, error-checked) and audio (steady rate). Separate types let the host schedule each without one ruining the other.

When a device is plugged in, enumeration begins. The host detects the port, resets it, reads the device descriptor through endpoint 0, assigns a unique address, then reads configuration, interface and endpoint descriptors. Descriptors state vendor and product IDs, class, power demand and endpoints. A class driver such as HID or mass storage then binds to the device.

blocks.text: USB 2.0 supplies bus power of 5 V and up to 500 mA per port, which is 2.5 W. A device may be bus-powered or self-powered. On-the-go (OTG) lets a phone act as a limited host for a keyboard or pen drive by swapping roles.

sections.h3: Parallel interfaces: eight bits and a handshake

blocks.text: A parallel interface sends several bits at once over separate wires, plus control lines. The Centronics printer port has eight data lines D0 to D7, a STROBE line, a BUSY line and an ACK line, often on a DB25 connector at the computer.

items: The host places one byte on D0 to D7.
The host asserts STROBE to say the byte is valid.
The printer asserts BUSY while it takes the byte.
The printer pulses ACK when it is ready for the next byte.
The host removes STROBE and can place the next byte.

blocks.text: IEEE 1284 standardized the port and added faster modes, but its compatibility mode is Centronics. A GPIO parallel port is simpler: a microcontroller writes eight bits to a port register for an LCD, often with a strobe but with no ACK line.

Parallel is not automatically faster. Skew, where bits arrive at slightly different times, crosstalk between wires and many pins limit cable length. IEEE 488, also called GPIB, uses 8-bit parallel with a handshake and up to 15 devices on one bus; it was common for lab instruments, and only a few universities teach its details now.

examples.question: A USB 2.0 full-speed bulk transfer sends a 1 MB file at 12 Mbit/s. Ignore protocol overhead. Find the transfer time in seconds.
steps: Convert 1 MB to bytes: 1 MB = 1,048,576 bytes in binary units.
Convert bytes to bits: 1,048,576 bytes × 8 bits/byte = 8,388,608 bits.
Convert the rate to bits per second: 12 Mbit/s = 12 × 10⁶ bit/s = 12,000,000 bit/s.
Time = bits ÷ rate = 8,388,608 ÷ 12,000,000 = 0.699 s (rounded to three decimal places).
examples.answer: The 1 MB file takes about 0.699 s at 12 Mbit/s.
examples.check:
mb = 1_048_576
bits = mb * 8
rate = 12_000_000
time = bits / rate
print(bits)
print(round(time, 3))

traps: USB is not peer-to-peer except with OTG. The host schedules all transfers; two devices cannot talk directly.
Full speed is 12 Mbit/s and high speed is 480 Mbit/s. Saying USB 2.0 is always 480 Mbit/s ignores full and low speed devices on the same bus.
1 MB is 1,048,576 bytes = 8,388,608 bits, not 8,000,000 bits. Using decimal megabytes changes the transfer time.
Parallel sends many bits at once, but it is not a faster UART. Skew and crosstalk limit cable length, and a GPIO parallel port may have no handshake at all.
Match the transfer type to the job: keyboard uses interrupt, audio uses isochronous, storage uses bulk, enumeration uses control. Examiners test this matching.

quiz.q: What bus power does USB 2.0 supply to a device?
quiz.a: 5 V and up to 500 mA per port, about 2.5 W.

quiz.q: Why must a USB device wait for the host to start a transfer?
quiz.a: USB is host-controlled: the host schedules all transactions, assigns addresses and polls endpoints, so no device can transmit on its own.

quiz.q: A USB full-speed bulk transfer sends 2 MB at 12 Mbit/s. Ignoring overhead, find the transfer time.
Match interrupt and isochronous transfers to a keyboard and a USB speaker, and explain the choice.
quiz.a: A keyboard uses interrupt: small data, bounded latency and retries are useful. A USB speaker uses isochronous: it needs reserved bandwidth and a steady rate, and dropped audio samples are not retried.

quiz.q: In a Centronics parallel port, name the eight data lines and three handshake or status lines.
quiz.a: Data lines D0 to D7; STROBE, BUSY and ACK.

quiz.q: Why is a parallel cable with eight data lines not automatically faster than a serial link?
quiz.a: Skew and crosstalk between lines limit clock rate and cable length; parallel transfers can stall waiting for the slowest bit, while a serial link needs fewer pins and can run at a high rate.

quiz.q: A GPIO port writes 0x5A to an 8-bit LCD data bus. How many data lines are high?
quiz.a: 0x5A = 0101 1010 in binary. Four bits are 1, so four data lines are high.

quiz.q: A designer wants to connect 15 lab instruments on one digital bus. Which parallel standard fits, and what limits it?
quiz.a: IEEE 488, also called GPIB, fits: 8-bit parallel, a handshake and up to 15 devices. Cable length and data rate are limited compared with modern serial buses.

beyond: Not for the exam. USB4 and USB Type-C with Power Delivery now carry data and substantial power over one connector, and device classes let one driver serve many products. Parallel printer ports have largely moved to USB or network links, while GPIB survives in older lab benches. Search next for USB 2.0 specification, USB Power Delivery, IEEE 1284 and IEEE 488 if you meet legacy hardware.
